feedback: If a learner finds the wishbone in all three, affirm: 'The wishbone you pull at a chicken dinner — a dinosaur had one too; that is the furcula.'
If a learner names only one shared feature, prompt them to look again at the feet and bones to reach at least two.
If a learner jumps to 'birds are dinosaurs' without pointing to features, ask them to show you the matching bones first so the claim rests on evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Birds and theropod dinosaurs share the same body parts (wishbone, hollow bones, three-toed feet), which is evidence that birds belong inside the theropod dinosaur group — a conclusion the learner reaches feature by feature rather than being told.
learnerActions: Examine three images or models side by side: a small feathered raptor (left), Archaeopteryx (middle), and a modern pigeon (right).
Locate the pigeon's wishbone (furcula), then find and point to the matching fused collarbone in the raptor and Archaeopteryx (its shape varies, from V- or U-shaped to boomerang-shaped).
Repeat for hollow (pneumatic) bones and the three main forward-pointing toes, naming each shared feature aloud or in writing before being told the conclusion.
Record a list of at least two skeletal features that a pigeon and a theropod such as Velociraptor or T. rex share.
Only after collecting the evidence, state in your own words why birds can be called living dinosaurs.
activities.title: Find the shared bones: raptor, Archaeopteryx, pigeon

feedback: If a learner lists only bird-like traits, ask what in its mouth, hands and tail looks like an earlier non-avian theropod (teeth, clawed fingers, long bony tail).
If a learner calls it 'the missing link' or 'the single ancestor of all birds', clarify it is one transitional form illustrating the pattern, not necessarily a direct sole ancestor.
Affirm reasoning that connects the mixture of traits to a lineage caught mid-change.
activities.intendedInsight: Transitional forms like Archaeopteryx are real and expected: a single animal can carry a mixture of older features seen in non-avian theropods and newer features seen in modern birds, documenting change over time.
learnerActions: Look closely at a reconstruction of Archaeopteryx (about 150 million years old, Late Jurassic).
Sort its features into two columns: traits like modern birds (flight feathers, feathered wings) and traits like earlier non-avian theropods (teeth, clawed fingers, long bony tail).
Explain in a sentence or two why a fossil that shows both sets of traits at once is called a 'transitional' fossil.
Discuss why such a creature is expected evidence for evolution, not a strange exception.
activities.title: Archaeopteryx as a mosaic

feedback: If a learner says the feathers were for flying, point to the non-flying feathered dinosaur: feathers came first and served other purposes such as insulation or display.
If a learner still equates feathers with birds, revisit the feathered dinosaur skeleton that is clearly not a bird.
activities.intendedInsight: Feathers evolved before flight and were present on many non-avian dinosaurs, so feathers are not unique to birds; they were later co-opted for flight.
learnerActions: Study an image of a feathered non-avian dinosaur that could NOT fly (for example a small flightless feathered theropod among the exceptionally preserved specimens from the Liaoning deposits in China), showing feather impressions around a clearly non-bird skeleton.
Note the evidence scientists use to infer that this animal could not fly (for example short arms and simple, fluffy rather than flight-shaped feathers), yet see that it had feathers anyway.
Suggest what feathers might have been useful for before flight (for example insulation/warmth or display).
Write a sentence explaining why 'feathers mean it was a bird' is not correct.
activities.title: Feathers before flight

feedback: If a learner says 'they all died out so birds can't be dinosaurs', correct it: the non-avian dinosaurs died out but one lineage survives as birds, so not all dinosaurs are extinct.
If a learner accepts the link but gives no evidence, ask them to name a fossil (Archaeopteryx or Chinese feathered dinosaurs) and two shared features (hollow bones, wishbone, three-toed feet).

If a learner says birds came from the 'bird-hipped' dinosaurs (e.g. Stegosaurus or Triceratops), correct the irony: birds arose from the lizard-hipped theropods; the hip-group names describe hip shape, not ancestry.
If a learner calls pterosaurs dinosaurs or bird ancestors, clarify that pterosaurs are neither dinosaurs nor bird ancestors; bird flight arose within theropods.
activities.intendedInsight: Birds are a surviving theropod lineage: only the non-avian dinosaurs became extinct, and the bird–dinosaur link is supported by fossils and shared anatomy, not just asserted.
learnerActions: Respond to a friend who says: 'Birds can't be related to dinosaurs — dinosaurs were huge scaly reptiles and they all died out, but birds are small and have feathers.'
Write what you would say back, citing at least one transitional or feathered fossil and at least two shared skeletal features.
State clearly which dinosaurs went extinct and which survived: the non-avian dinosaurs died out, while one lineage lives on as birds.
Finish with a formal statement: birds are classified inside the theropod dinosaurs, so the dinosaurs never fully died out.
activities.title: Which dinosaurs survived? (defend the claim)
